sentences.text: Armadillosuchus was a large and robust sphagesaurid crocodylomorph that reached a total length of about 2 meters.
It is considered one of the best-armored notosuchians due to its distinctive body armor made of small bony plates called osteoderms.
The animal possessed a robust, slightly flattened skull that maintained the oreinirostral form typical of Notosuchians.
The holotype specimen UFRJ DG 303-R is a well-preserved partial skeleton including the entire skull, neck, cervical osteoderms, front torso, and a nearly complete left forelimb.
Marinho and Carvalho also described a second, less complete paratype specimen consisting of partial upper and lower jaws.
The back was covered by armor with flexible bands and rigid protectors similar to an armadillo, reflecting the genus name meaning "armadillo crocodile".
Its teeth were heterodont, creating powerful, scissor-like jaws capable of chewing food.

Unlike modern crocodilians, Sharpey's fibers ran perpendicular to the outer surface of the osteoderms, suggesting they were deeply embedded in the skin under a leathery dermis for increased flexibility.
The genus Armadillosuchus was described by Marinho and Carvalho in 2009, with the type species Armadillosuchus arrudai named by the same authors.
The species name arrudai honors João Tadeu Arruda for his contributions to the paleontology of the region.
It was described in February 2009 from the Upper Cretaceous Bauru Basin in Brazil.
Based on its teeth and size, Armadillosuchus is believed to have been an omnivore that ate invertebrates, plants, and possibly scavenged.

Wear facets on the teeth suggest the animal used a back-and-forth chewing motion similar to Sphagesaurus, and it is possible the animal occasionally scavenged dried carcasses, which may have caused the observed tooth wear.
The animal may have used gastroliths to assist in grinding food alongside its specialized teeth.
Researchers suggest that Armadillosuchus's well-developed forelimbs may have allowed it to burrow, potentially helping it regulate its body temperature.
The osteoderms may have helped absorb and retain heat during basking, allowing high activity levels without direct sunlight.
Due to its singular morphology, it is believed to have had a subterranean lifestyle.
Fossils were found in the Adamantina Formation of the Bauru Basin in Brazil and date to approximately 70 million years ago.

In a 2026 review, Kitayama and Bertini provisionally proposed that Armadillosuchus arrudai is a junior synonym of Sphagesaurus huenei, arguing that the features distinguishing Armadillosuchus arrudai were insufficiently diagnostic and might represent intraspecific variation or deformation.

The reconstruction of the armor on the back of the body remains difficult due to only isolated material being known, and it is debated whether terrestrial Notosuchians like Armadillosuchus regulated temperature like modern monitor lizards rather than like modern crocodilians.
